body.text: Since taking office in 2022, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has articulated three main risks weighing on the country’s economy. First, major power tensions, particularly between the US and China, are spilling over into trade and technology. Second, punitive tariffs under the second Trump administration and the weakening of the multilateral trading order, including the weaponisation of trade measures. Third, supply chain disruptions arising from a range of factors, from geopolitical conflicts such as the Hormuz crisis to climate events such as El Niño.

In the face of these headwinds, how does Malaysia see ASEAN’s role in navigating them? What constitutes the floor and ceiling — that is, minimum expectations of ASEAN and the bloc’s best-case performance respectively? Can ASEAN deliver, or as Malaysians would say, ASEAN boleh?

Malaysia’s geoeconomic strategy often leans on three planks: diversify economic relationships, deepen economic integration and hold the line on multilateralism. This is in line with the State of Southeast Asia 2026 Survey published by ISEAS. When asked how ASEAN can enhance resilience and respond to rising protectionism and nationalism, Malaysian responses were relatively high in various categories: expediting economic integration (43.8 per cent), increasing intra-ASEAN trade and investment (32 per cent), and building alternative supply chains (24.7 per cent). These geoeconomic goals, if pursued with resolve and resource commitments, would give Malaysia greater capacity to weather shocks, more options over whom it trades and partners with, and more leverage than Malaysia could command alone.

Lately, Putrajaya has introduced a fourth plank: building trusted supply chains, given how geoeconomic pressure has evolved. When US-China tensions initially sharpened, Malaysia was optimistic that Southeast Asia would benefit by capturing ‘China+1’ and ‘friendshoring’ investments as multinational firms relocated production out of China to circumvent US tariffs. But increasingly, Malaysia is concerned that it will be caught in the crossfire because US trade policy has evolved beyond product origin (for example, whether a product was made in China) to target Chinese entities globally through, for instance, extraterritorial export controls and transshipment rules. Consequently, Putrajaya is looking into preserving neutrality and building an ecosystem that can accommodate Western and Chinese trade, capital and supply chains concurrently.

ASEAN already delivers on the first three priorities. The bloc continues to deepen economic linkages within ASEAN and with external partners, including through the upgraded ASEAN-China Free Trade Agreement 3.0 signed in October last year. Pacts like the Digital Economy Framework Agreement, concluded in November 2026, and ongoing work on the ASEAN Power Grid facilitate openness and connectivity in new and emerging sectors. When it comes to building trusted supply chains, ASEAN’s primary contribution lies in helping to anchor geopolitical neutrality, given that strategic trade rules remain decided at the national level.

Where Malaysia sees room to raise the floor is in the scale and reach of those links, driven in part by Anwar’s considerable diplomatic capital. This brings both global connections and consequently, a broader political imagination of the partnerships and configurations that can be built around ASEAN. The ASEAN-GCC-China Summit, launched under Malaysia’s 2025 chairmanship, tied the bloc more closely to new centres of capital, demand, technology and energy. The 47th Summit pointed the same way: Brazil and South Africa, both BRICS members, joined as the Chairman’s guests. Anwar recalled that these emerging economies had asked why they could not engage ASEAN, something he called “a new beginning” for the grouping’s “relative centrality”.

Views about the floor do vary. Integration, diversification and regionalism form the baseline across the political spectrum. But Opposition MP Wan Fayhsal, who holds the shadow Foreign Minister post, views the expected bare minimum as greater operational resilience that leaves members “better informed, less isolated and more credible” rather than high-level summitry that convenes a range of partners. In practice, this entails greater information sharing, joint assessments of supply chain exposure and resolving internal conflicts and tensions to create a more united front against external pressure.

As Wan Fayhsal said to this author, “My concern is that the government expects too much from ASEAN as a diplomatic platform, while asking too little of it as a mechanism for practical coordination. Hosting successful summits and keeping good relations with the major powers both matter, but neither automatically translates into greater bargaining power or real protection for Malaysian businesses.”

While the ceiling is less explicitly articulated compared to the floor, Anwar’s speeches suggest that expectations turn on greater clarity about strategic flux and the ability to shape the geoeconomic landscape.

Yet the fundamental tension is that ASEAN remains, to a significant extent, a price-taker rather than a price-maker. While the bloc consistently defends the multilateral trading order and repudiates power politics, member states cannot realistically unplug from either Western or Chinese trade, capital and technology circuits, and would be better served by a more proactive, anticipatory regionalism. This would defang the risks of dependence on those circuits being used as leverage and enable ASEAN to structurally adapt to policy shifts and systemic disruptions, including those emanating from Washington and Beijing, before they fully materialise.

The ASEAN Geoeconomic Task Force (AGTF), which was co-chaired by Malaysia and launched during its 2025 ASEAN Chairmanship, represents an attempt to shift the bloc in the above direction. For instance, the AGTF recommended that the bloc coordinate on rules-of-origin and digitised certification to give member states a way to proactively prove genuine local processing, rather than defensively react to, for example, US transshipment accusations.

Another initiative launched under Malaysia’s chairmanship, the ASEAN Framework for Integrated Semiconductor Supply Chain (AFISS), attempts to shape the geoeconomic landscape through regional industrial policy. AFISS is a play toward “semiconductor sovereignty” — reorganising supply chains around member states’ comparative advantages to build a vertically integrated production bloc. By positioning itself as a unified, politically neutral ecosystem rather than a collection of fragmented suppliers, ASEAN could gain the leverage required to negotiate trade terms safely with both superpowers, thereby safeguarding the sector against external technological chokepoints, supply disruptions and fragmented national policies.

This is not the first time Malaysia has pushed for regional industrial policy in a strategic sector, as seen in the ASEAN Defence Industry Collaboration proposed in 2010 and endorsed in 2011. Across administrations, Malaysia has long recognised the value of pooling regional capabilities in sectors where dependence on external suppliers creates strategic vulnerabilities. What has changed is that such vulnerabilities are no longer confined to traditional security domains — economic interdependence itself has become a primary source of coercive leverage.

Malaysia’s views of ASEAN and its efforts during the 2025 chairmanship to advance the bloc’s geoeconomic agenda reflect growing expectations across the region for ASEAN to play a more active role in navigating economic uncertainty and great-power competition. A common refrain, as re-articulated by Wan Fayhsal, is that “good ideas should not end when a chairmanship ends”; the AGTF and joint Foreign and Economic Ministers Meetings were endorsed as something “worth continuing, whichever coalition governs Malaysia” after the upcoming national elections.

Yet these evolving expectations also highlight underlying tensions. In seeking to protect itself against the securitisation of trade, capital and technology, ASEAN risks reinforcing the very logic it hopes to resist. Measures to build trusted supply chains may help members withstand external scrutiny, but could also deepen the tendency to view economic relationships through a security lens, while imposing mounting compliance costs on businesses seeking to prove their trustworthiness to different trading partners. This is a tension Singapore will have to navigate as it takes over as 2027 ASEAN Chair, including while steering any potential initiatives for a more comprehensive approach to economic security and resilience.

As to what can further enhance the region’s geoeconomic capabilities, the view from Malaysia was that ASEAN needs to close the generational gap. Senior officials from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, as well as Wan Fayhsal, shared a quiet anxiety over generational continuity. The upcoming cohort of leaders, technocrats and business executives inherit a complex regional architecture without having lived through the historical friction, diplomatic crises, and compromises that forged it. Without an experiential understanding of how hard-won ASEAN’s cohesion is, there is a risk that a younger generation would take ASEAN’s neutrality for granted and fail to appreciate why collective regional resilience matters when major-power pressure mounts. ASEAN’s 60th anniversary, which coincides with Singapore’s chairmanship, offers a timely opportunity to bring that history to life.
